Susan B. Anthony. Born in 1820, the American women's rights activist who spent more than fifty years fighting for women's suffrage. She would die in 1906, fourteen years before the Nineteenth Amendment passed.

Anthony co-founded the National Woman Suffrage Association with Elizabeth Cady Stanton in 1869, after tensions within the broader women's movement over tactics and strategy. She became the primary public orator of the suffrage cause, traveling extensively across America and internationally, giving speeches year after year.

In 1872, she illegally voted in the presidential election in her hometown of Rochester, New York. She was arrested, convicted, and fined one hundred dollars. She refused to pay. This act of civil disobedience, alongside her extensive public speaking, made her the face of the suffrage movement.

She and Stanton co-authored The History of Woman Suffrage, a three-volume work created with Matilda Joslyn Gage. It became the authoritative record of the movement. Anthony called for a federal amendment to grant women the vote—what would become the Nineteenth Amendment, ratified four years after her death.

She never married, dedicating her entire adult life to the cause. Late in life, she reflected that she had "not a regret except that I have not lived long enough to vote." Yet her fifty years of work laid the foundation for the victory that followed.
